# Kin Jay · กินเจ — the Vegetarian Festival

The Vegetarian Festival, 10–18 October 2026: the yellow 齋 flag, what stays off the plate, the menu, the shrines, halls and jay kitchens of Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai, Thailand's vegetarian groups, and the legends.

English: https://motdang.net/sites/kin-jay/
Thai: https://motdang.net/sites/kin-jay/th/
Also: https://nanobotco.github.io/kin-jay/

## The nine days, 2026

- Saturday 10 October · day 1: Bangkok, Yaowarat Yaowarat opens, 16:00Korat Shrine rites, 16:09Phuket Nine lamps up on the pole since last nightChiang Mai Guan Im foundation rites; J Food Festival at both Centrals
- Sunday 11 October · day 2: Phuket Naka shrine procession, 07:30
- Monday 12 October · day 3: Phuket Sapam shrine procession, 07:00. At dusk: feeding the five heavenly armies
- Tuesday 13 October · day 4: Phuket Sam Kong shrine, 06:45Korat Procession through the city, 08:29
- Wednesday 14 October · day 5: Phuket Tha Rua shrine, 06:09Krabi Jay keepers gather on Maha Rat Road
- Thursday 15 October · day 6: Phuket Bang Niao shrine, 06:00Hat Yai Procession, lion and dragon dancesKorat Zodiac bridge crossing, 19:19
- Friday 16 October · day 7: Phuket Jui Tui shrine, 08:00. Offering to the stars, about 20:00Phang Nga Procession
- Saturday 17 October · day 8: Phuket Kathu, the oldest shrine, 06:45
- Sunday 18 October · day 9: Phuket Lo Rong shrine, 07:00. 22:30: the gods go to the sea at Saphan HinEverywhere Jay ends at midnight

- 9 Oct 2026: Clean-out day (lang thong): strict keepers eat jay the day before, to start clean.
- 10–18 Oct 2026: The nine days, 1st to 9th of the ninth Chinese month.
- Night of 18 Oct: Jay ends after midnight, into the 19th.
- 30 Sep–8 Oct 2027: Next year, per Kapook's 2027 calendar.

## Read the flag: 齋 · เจ

Hang the yellow flag and you are telling the street: nothing from an animal in this food. Chinese signs write 齋. Thai signs spell it เจ.
- Readings: jay in Thai, chai in Hokkien, zhāi in Mandarin, chay in Vietnamese; simplified Chinese 斋
- Yellow: once kept for royalty and exorcists, so read as the colour of Buddhism and the precepts (Thai Wikipedia)
- Red: good fortune
- White: what keepers wear

## Jay or not? Cook it.

No meat, fish, egg, milk, honey, fish sauce or oyster sauce. No pungent five, either: that is the line between jay and vegetarian.
- Garlic: กระเทียม
- Onions of every kind: หอม: spring onion, shallot, onion
- Garlic chives: กุยช่าย
- Chinese garlic, lak kiao: หลักเกียว, a small single-clove garlic
- Tobacco leaf, or coriander: depending on whose list
- Also: No alcohol. The strict cook in pots that have never held meat, keep the five precepts, keep their speech gentle and abstain from sex.

## Order jay

- Phat mi sua jay (stir-fried longevity noodles): Thin Fujian wheat noodles, fried with cabbage, shiitake and tofu. The festival's must-have.
- Tom chap chai jay (mixed-vegetable stew): Daikon, bok choy, cabbage and celery with tofu. Hokkien for 'mixed vegetables'.
- Sup yuea phai jay (bamboo-fungus soup): Clear hot soup of bamboo fungus.
- Khao tom jay with kana chai (rice porridge and pickled greens): Porridge on all day, with kana chai, a Chinese pickled green.
- Khao phat nam liap jay (fried rice with Chinese black olive): Rice fried with salted Chinese black olive.
- Kaeng khiao wan jay (jay green curry): Coconut milk, vegetables, tofu. No shrimp paste, no garlic in the paste.
- Khanom chin nam ya jay (rice noodles with jay curry sauce): Fermented rice noodles under jay curry. Free at Pung Tao Kong in 2023.
- Hor mok jay (steamed curry in banana leaf): Steamed curry custard in banana leaf, with tofu or mushroom.
- Rat na jay (noodles in gravy): Wide noodles, thick gravy, baby corn, kale.
- Kuai chap yuan jay (rolled rice-noodle soup): Rolled rice noodles in clear broth, with tofu.
- Phat makhuea jay (stir-fried aubergine): Long aubergine, stir-fried.
- Larb jay (minced salad, jay): Tofu, mushroom or fried flour, dressed as larb. Sold at Warorot in 2025.
- Nam phrik num jay (northern green-chilli dip): Grilled green chillies, pounded, no fish sauce or garlic.
- Mu daeng jay (red 'pork', from gluten): Gluten or soy protein made to look like Chinese red pork.
- Tao hu thot, phueak thot (fried tofu, fried taro): Tofu, taro, daikon and corn, fried.
- Fong tao hu thot (fried tofu skin): Skin lifted off hot soy milk, dried, fried crisp.
- Po pia thot jay (fried spring rolls): KTC's easy festival snack.
- Nam tao hu (soy milk): Hot soy milk, often with grains.
- Tao huai nam khing (tofu pudding in ginger syrup): Soft tofu in hot ginger syrup.
- Bua loi phueak (taro dumplings in coconut milk): Taro dumplings in warm coconut milk.
- Kluai buat chi (bananas in coconut milk): Bananas simmered in sweet coconut milk.

## Eat jay in Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai

Tap a dot. Every place opens on Mot Dang.
- Guan Im Dhamma Dan Foundation, 9–18 Oct 2026, Mueang Samut Road, Chiang Mai: Rites led by Chinese monks from Wat Muen Puttha Mettakhunaram, Mae Chan. White clothes for the rites; 053-235-968. (https://www.chiangmainews.co.th/social/4146691/)
- Thailand J Food Festival 2026, 9–18 Oct 2026, Central Chiang Mai and Central Chiang Mai Airport: Jay dishes, a J Market of more than twenty brands, and workshops. (https://www.thethaipress.com/2026/171849)
- Pung Tao Kong Shrine, 2025: all nine days, by Warorot, Chiang Mai: Free jay meals at 11:00–12:00 and 16:00–17:00. No 2026 notice seen by 7 Oct. (https://www.cmhy.city/event/1618-You-are-invited-to-join-the-Vegetarian-Festival-at-the-Pung-Tao-Kong-Shrine-Chiang-Mai-2025)
- Warorot market, 2025, Kad Luang, Chiang Mai: Yellow flags across the market; one jay stall cooked about twenty dishes a day at 35–40 baht a box. (https://www.chiangmainews.co.th/news/chiangmai/3797300/)
- Kuang Meng Foundation free kitchen, 2025, Mae Sai, Chiang Rai: A free jay kitchen, 11:30–14:00: rice, glass-noodle stir-fry, tofu soup, pumpkin curry, ginger and soy drinks. (https://www.lemon8-app.com/@viewolet/7563606336190841352?region=th)
- Jay food centre, Wiang, 2023, Mueang Chiang Rai: Open 07:00–15:00 through the festival, meals at 30, 40 and 45 baht. (https://www.chiangmainews.co.th/news/chiangrai/3114216/)

## Go: festivals across Thailand

- Phuket, 9–18 Oct 2026: The pole goes up 9 Oct at about 17:09; eight shrine processions, one a day, 11–18 Oct; fire-walking, the bridge-crossing and the send-off to the sea at Saphan Hin on the night of the 18th. On Thailand's national intangible-heritage list since 2018. (https://www.dailynews.co.th/news/6253434/)
- Bangkok, Yaowarat, 9–18 Oct 2026: At the Yaowarat arch: jay food down both sides of the road, palanquins from 22 Yaowarat shrines, road closed 10 Oct 16:00–22:00 for the opening. (https://www.thansettakij.com/lifestyle/travel-shopping/670700)
- Nakhon Ratchasima, 10–18 Oct 2026: The 20th year at the Thao Suranari monument; procession 13 Oct, the twelve-zodiac bridge 15 Oct at 19:19. (https://www.thansettakij.com/lifestyle/travel-shopping/670740)
- Hat Yai, Songkhla, 9–18 Oct 2026: More than 108 jay food shops at Suan Yom Suphasan Rangsan; city procession 15 Oct; lion and dragon dances 15–16 Oct. (https://www.dailynews.co.th/news/6251835/)
- Trang, 10–18 Oct 2026: Shrines across the province: charity kitchens, processions, fire-walking. (https://www.dailynews.co.th/news/6251835/)
- Krabi, 10–18 Oct 2026: Shrine rites and jay kitchens in town; the gathering of jay keepers on Maha Rat Road, 14 Oct. (https://www.dailynews.co.th/news/6251835/)
- Phang Nga, 10–18 Oct 2026: Nine shrines in nine days; procession 16 Oct. (https://www.dailynews.co.th/news/6253434/)
- Nakhon Sawan, October: On the province's calendar at Na Pha shrine, Mueang. (https://www.dailynews.co.th/news/6251835/)
- Nonthaburi, 9–18 Oct 2026: A jay festival at Outlet Square, Muang Thong Thani. (https://www.dailynews.co.th/news/6251835/)

## Who eats jay

- Shrine halls (โรงเจ · ศาลเจ้า · อ๊าม): They run the festival. Over a hundred Nine Emperor and Dou Mu temples in 20+ provinces, registered as charities. (https://has.hcu.ac.th/jspui/bitstream/123456789/3938/1/Big-Dipper-belief-and-Thai-Chinese-belief-ritual-of.pdf)
- Mahayana monks (จีนนิกาย · อนัมนิกาย): Chinese-lineage monks skip meat, egg, dairy and the pungent five. The Vietnamese-lineage Annam Nikaya: 27 temples, 3 monasteries. (https://th.wikipedia.org/wiki/อนัมนิกาย)
- Santi Asoke (สันติอโศก): Phra Bodhirak's movement, apart from the Sangha council since 1975. Strict vegetarian, one meal a day, 27 centres (2007), five in the north. (https://aseas.univie.ac.at/index.php/aseas/article/download/2481/2070)
- Yiguandao (อนุตตรธรรม · 一貫道): A Chinese religion from 1800s Shandong. Vegetarian eating is a core teaching. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiguandao)
- Thai Plum Village (หมู่บ้านพลัม): Thich Nhat Hanh's monastery at Pak Chong. Every meal vegetarian. (https://www.thaiplumvillage.org/visitor-guide)
- Sikh gurdwaras (คุรุดวารา): About twenty in Thailand. Phahurat's Siri Guru Singh Sabha feeds anyone a free vegetarian breakfast; Chiang Mai's dates from 1907. (https://thailandmagazine.com/bangkok/temples/sikh-temple/)
- Theravada laypeople (ฆราวาส): A sizeable minority eat vegetarian, Thailand and Sri Lanka above all. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist_vegetarianism)

## Legends

### The nine stars (doctrine)

The Nine Emperor Gods are the Big Dipper's seven stars plus two no one can see, sons of Dou Mu. Honour them, live longer. The Thai telling: seven past Buddhas and two bodhisattvas, the nine planets. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Emperor_Gods_Festival)

### The opera troupe at Kathu (local tradition)

Fever hits the tin mines of Kathu, Phuket. A Chinese opera troupe falls sick, blames its skipped vegetarian rites, keeps them, and recovers. The town follows. 1825, says the governor; 1827, says Thai Wikipedia; after 1855, says a Chula thesis. (https://www.thaipost.net/news-update/668677/)

### The Ming loyalists (folk legend)

White-clad fighters eat no meat or pungent plants, chant spells against Manchu guns, and lose. The festival remembers them. A Huachiew study finds six versions across Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore. (https://has.hcu.ac.th/jspui/bitstream/123456789/3938/1/Big-Dipper-belief-and-Thai-Chinese-belief-ritual-of.pdf)

### The nine princes of Jiangxi (folk legend)

A leper beggar at rich Li Huakai's gate orders nine days of jay to stop a coming disaster. Li obeys, the town follows, the disaster passes. (https://th.wikipedia.org/wiki/เทศกาลกินเจ)

### Lao Seng's mother (folk legend)

A drunk dreams of his dead mother: she is happy on Mount Putuo because she ate only jay. He sets out, breaks his vow on the road, and still finds her floating above the incense pot. (https://th.wikipedia.org/wiki/เทศกาลกินเจ)

### Emperor Wu of Liang (history)

From 502 the Liang emperor eats one vegetarian meal a day and swaps the goats, pigs and cattle of the imperial sacrifice for animals moulded from flour. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Wu_of_Liang)

### Devadatta's five rules (Pali canon)

Devadatta asks the Buddha to ban fish and meat for monks. The Buddha refuses; Devadatta splits the Sangha. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devadatta)

## Words

- เจ (jay · 齋): Food with nothing from an animal and none of the five pungent plants; also the observance itself.
- กินเจ (kin jay · 食齋): To keep jay. In Phuket the older word is chia chai, 'eat vegetables'.
- ล้างท้อง (lang thong): The clean-out day before the nine days.
- ออกเจ (ok jay): Coming out of jay after the last night.
- โรงเจ (rong jay): A jay hall: a Chinese religious hall with its own kitchen.
- อ๊าม (am · 庵): Phuket's word for a shrine.
- โกเต้ง (ko teng · 高燈): The tall lantern pole raised to begin the festival, carrying the nine lamps.
- กิ๋วอ๋องไต่เต่ (kiu ong tai te · 九皇大帝): The Nine Emperor Gods.
- ม้าทรง (ma song): A spirit medium, 'the horse the god rides'.
- อิ้วเก้ง (iu keng · 游境): The procession that carries the gods through the streets.
- โก้ยโห้ย (koi hoi): Fire-walking.
- โก้ยห่าน (koi han): Crossing the bridge: a rite of cleansing at the shrine.
- ผักฉุน (phak chun): The five pungent plants jay leaves out.
- หมี่กึง (mi kueng · 麵筋): Wheat gluten, the base of jay pork and duck.
- โปรตีนเกษตร (protein kaset): Textured soy protein, dried in chunks.
- ปิ่นโต (pinto): A stacked tiffin carrier; shrine kitchens fill them during the festival.
